messages.subject: feature request for rstan
parts:
Hi!
 
I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this
 
attach(stan_data)
stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
detach(stan_data)
 
Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like
 
myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }
 
My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.
 
I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.
 
Best,
 
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request for rstan
parts:
We're about to undertake a major overhaul on the RStan interface,
so now is the time to get feature requests in!

Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
read a global variable in the body of a function. Perhaps not
the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
this kind of scoping.

But R is nothing if not flexible. Maybe you'd be happier with
a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
to a "factory" function that creates the init function. For example,

init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
}

and then call with

stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));

Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
of Stan:

> factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })

> data <- list(alpha=10)

> alpha
Error: object 'alpha' not found

> init_fun <- factory(data)

> init_fun()
[1] 10

You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.

Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?

- Bob

My own preference is not to have complex defaults and not under
any circumstances to play with default environments for user-supplied
functions. The former so everything's easy to doc and test and understand
(though perhaps not so easy to use in a single step) and the latter
so that the behavior is predictible to R users who might themselves
be monkeying with environments as you did.

But I'm not the only one with my hands on the steering wheel of the
Stan bus. And I'm more concerned that the lower-level functionality is
implemented cleanly than the high-level calls (for instance, "stan()" calls
compilers, data readers, and then one or more chain runners --- it's
the thing stan() calls that I'm most concerned with).

That %in% function looks really useful!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request for rstan
parts:
Let me rewrite your request following Andrew's (and hence
Stan's) notation.

You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and
you want to sample from a posterior p(alpha,beta | y)
by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.

Fair enough --- we'd love to make that easy to do. In fact,
it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
proposal.

I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
the next version (more below).

WARNING: I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
but for everyone else's sake: because beta now looks like "data" to
Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta
changes, it changes the posterior from which Stan is trying to sample.
This is an issue because our adaptation assumes that we're
only trying to adapt to a single posterior.

In R, we are going to be breaking the stan() command down and exposing
some more primitive operations:

* compiling a model: translates model from Stan to C++ and compiles
a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
of the model

* create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
code

We also want to be able to specify all the inputs and outputs including
adaptation, so that you can

* extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters

* start a sampler with given adaptation parameters

Most of the time in our algorithm is spent computing gradients.
The faster that goes, the faster everything goes. If the adaptation
gets messed up, you'll have to intentionally slow everything down by
forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.

The fact that interpreted R is snail slow isn't usually a problem if
you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting. But
you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
computation using R. But then if you have a good general technique
prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.

- Bob

I don't see anything you're missing, so maybe Michael
will chime in.

I don't understand why Michael's talking about computing marginal
distributions in closed form --- we just have Bayes's rule and compute
everything up to a constant. I think that'll work for your
proposal.

that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
Gibbs easy to implement. The fact that we don't do that is
why we don't have any discrete sampling.

Gibbs updates any time soon. And if you had to implement full Gibbs this way,
as in trying to code up BUGS in Stan, it'd be too much copying to be efficient
unless there were only a few blocks.

- Bob

parts:
Hi!

Since you asked for features:

- a facility to simulate from a posterior would be nice, i.e. currently I loop over each draw of a posterior and fire up stan for each draw; the posterior should come either from a stanfit object or an array (I may want to mess around with the posterior before I simulate).

- some way to access the data from within the init function, i.e. like Ben pointed out; not so urgent, I am happy to live with the environment stuff I digged up in R.

- I saw you intend to parallelize things easily for users; here it would be great to keep things as flexible as possible (most people use some openmp, some MPI, and ...); concerning seeding I think it would be best to go with one stan seed which is the same for all chains, but different chain_ids; one more note: I keep reading that parallelization is not possible under windows which is not true, it is just different, i.e. you need to use "cl <- makeCluster(ncpu, type=ifelse(.Platform$OS.type == "windows", "PSOCK", "FORK"))"; but this PSOCK cluster needs to be handled with a bit of care (seeds, data exporting!); I use this with foreach which I find useful, but other will disagree here I guess

- consider to make the model chaching option configurable via the options interface from R so that users can set in their R profile if they like caching permanently on or not

- possibly consider to cache models in different compiled versions (fast/debug/NDEBUG) when they are requested in different flavors along the road

- I hope the current stan merge function stays, it is very useful as I run multiple chains on a cluster and each in a separate process which I merge at the end of the day

- Speeding up the monitor function would be great - I know you consider moving that bit into C++ to make it fast. If you could also write a function such that I can stick coda samples into it, that would even be better (sometimes I would like to do comparisons of Stan runs with JAGS/WinBUGS)

@ Bob: R is full of thousands of very convenient functions and I agree your closure type approach is programmatically much nicer (but the flow of my program does not go with it and after all it is just R - so who cares anyway).

Best,
Sebastian

Sebastian

- I hope the current stan merge function stays, it is very useful as I run multiple chains on a cluster and each in a separate process which I merge at the end of the day

Sebastian

On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 11:25:38 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I don't see anything you're missing, so maybe Michael
will chime in.

Ok, this is something I'm doing in an applied project so I would like to
hear if there are serious problems with it.

I don't understand why Michael's talking about computing marginal
distributions in closed form --- we just have Bayes's rule and compute
everything up to a constant.  I think that'll work for your
proposal.  

If we did limit models to DAGs a la BUGS, then there's more
that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
Gibbs easy to implement.  The fact that we don't do that is
why we don't have any discrete sampling.

And just to be clear about our goals, we're not planning on building these
Gibbs updates any time soon. And if you had to implement full Gibbs this way,
as in trying to code up BUGS in Stan, it'd be too much copying to be efficient
unless there were only a few blocks.

Yeah, a lot of copying.  I did a proof-of-concept a while ago which I'm pasting below.
Note that it currently does not work b/c I've changed the package code (and it requries
a library I have on github, which has also changed).  I am currently updating my examples
and I will link them here it in the next week or so to make it run-able.  For now it's an ugly mock-up...
but at least it makes my goals clear.  I think the ability to do a few big blocks will save me
and maybe others from writing NUTS by hand or writing the umpteenth version of slow code for doing an HLM.

library(Rux)
library(MASS)
library(rstan)


## From total marked population size (N), times of surveys (tos),
## survival probability (phi), and recapture probability (p),
## simulate times of ``births'', followed by the survival process
## (time of alive matrix, toaM), and the recapture process
## (time of recpature matrix, torM).  From these, calculate the
## list of times of recapture (tor) and the vector of times of
## death (tod).
tos <- 1:10
N <- 200
phi <- rep(.8,max(tos))
p <- 0.7
tbs <- rbinom(n=N, size=5, prob=.3)+1
toaM <- matrix(0,nrow=N, ncol=length(tos))
torM <- matrix(0,nrow=N, ncol=length(tos))

survive <- 0
die <- 0
recapture <- 0
miss <- 0

for ( i in 1:N ) {
  toaM[i,tbs[i]] <- 1
  torM[i,tbs[i]] <- 1
  for (j in (tbs[i]+1):max(tos) ) {
    toaM[i,j] <- toaM[i,j-1] *
      sample(x=c(0,1),size=1,replace=TRUE, prob=c(1-phi[j], phi[j]))
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (toaM[i,j-1] == 1)) survive <- survive + 1
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 0) && (toaM[i,j-1] == 1)) die <- die + 1

    torM[i,j] <- toaM[i,j] *
      sample(x=c(0,1),size=1,replace=TRUE, prob=c(1-p, p))
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (torM[i,j] == 1)) recapture <- recapture + 1
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (torM[i,j] == 0)) miss <- miss + 1

  }

}
tor <- apply(X=torM, MARGIN=1, FUN=function(x) {which(x==1)})
tod <- apply(X=toaM, MARGIN=1, FUN=function(x) {max(which(x==1))+1})
                                               

## Calculate realized survival and recapture probabilities.
true_phi <- survive/(survive + die)
true_p <-   recapture/(recapture + miss)


## Create matrices of (bad) initial values for the parameters of the
## survival (PHI) and recapture (P) processes.  These matrices are
## N x max(tos)*5 by default.
P <- matrix(data=0.6, nrow=N, ncol=max(tos)*5)
P[,(max(tos)+1):(max(tos)*5)] <- 0
PHI = 0.5

## Create a handle to the likelihood calculation and discrete slice
## sampler for time of death state.
o <- new("recapture_handle",
  times_of_surveys = tos,
  times_of_recaptures = tor,
  times_of_deaths = tod,
  known_deaths = rep(FALSE, N),
  PHI = PHI,
  P = P
)

## Calculate the initial likelihood, the time taken for this calculation
## should scale with N * K * 5.  
ll_calculation_time <- system.time(expr=o$log_likelihood)


## Create vectors to hold output from MCMC.
N_it <- 1000
o_accept <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_PHI <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_P <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_lpd <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)

## Stan model for simulating from PHI/P conditional on known
## birth, death, and recapture times for n tags.
stan_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> n_tags;
    int<lower=0> n_occasions;
    int<lower=0> tb[n_tags];
    int<lower=0> td[n_tags];
    int<lower=0, upper=1> recaptures[n_tags, n_occasions];

  }

  // Declare parameters for the linear models.
  parameters {
    real beta;
    real gamma;
  }

  // Rubber meets the road for linear model specification.
  transformed parameters {
    real PHI_logit[n_tags, 5*n_occasions];
    real P_logit[n_tags, 5*n_occasions];
    for ( tag in 1:n_tags ) { // indexing covers PHI/P
      for ( t in tb[tag]:(td[tag]-1) ) {
        PHI_logit[tag,t] <- beta;
        P_logit[tag,t] <- gamma;
      }
    }
  }
 model {

    // Priors for linear model coefficients.
    beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
    gamma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

    // Mark-recapture likelihood.
    for ( tag in 1:n_tags ) {
      for ( t in tb[tag]:(td[tag]-2) ) { // SURVIVES
        1 ~ bernoulli_logit(PHI_logit[tag,t]);
      }
      0 ~ bernoulli_logit(PHI_logit[tag,td[tag]-1]);  // DIES

      for ( t in (tb[tag]+1):min(n_occasions,td[tag]-1) ) {  // AVAILABLE
        recaptures[tag,t] ~ bernoulli_logit(P_logit[tag,t]);
      }
    }
  }

'

n_tags <- dim(o$recaptures)[1]
n_occ <- dim(o$recaptures)[2]
stan_fit <- NULL
stan_iter <- 200

stan_timing <- system.time({
for ( it in 1:N_it ) {
  print(it)
  ## Sample state:
  tds <- c(o$set_deaths(o$td))

  ## Sample PHI/P matrices:
  stan_fit <- stan(
    model_code=stan_code,
    data=list(
      n_tags = n_tags,
      n_occasions = n_occ,
      tb = tbs,
      td = tds,
      recaptures = o$recaptures
    ), fit=stan_fit,
    iter=stan_iter, chains=1, warmup=stan_iter/2,
    pars=c('beta','gamma')
  )

  ## Make matrices and re-assign them:
  stan_samples <- extract(stan_fit, permuted=TRUE)
  PHImat <- matrix(
    data=plogis(stan_samples$beta[stan_iter/2]),
    nrow=o$N, ncol=o$K*5, byrow=TRUE)
  Pmat <- matrix(
    data=plogis(stan_samples$gamma[stan_iter/2]),
    nrow=o$N, ncol=o$K*5, byrow=TRUE)
  Pmat[,(o$K+1):ncol(Pmat)] <- 0
  o$PHI <- PHImat
  o$P   <- Pmat

  ## Record for posterity
  o_PHI[it] = unique(c(o$PHI))
  o_P[it]   = max(unique(c(o$P)))
  o_lpd[it] = o$log_likelihood
}
})

plot(o_PHI, pch='*')
plot(o_lpd, pch='*')
plot(o_PHI, o_lpd, pch = '*')
plot(o_PHI, o_P, pch = '*')
abline(h=recapture/(recapture+miss))
abline(v=survive/(survive+die))

- Bob

parts:
Nothing is being written out to .csv format and
read back in. That would be super slow.
Everything communicates directly in memory through Rcpp.

Restricting the number of parameters output more efficiently
from the C++ Stan side is on our to-do list. But R should
already be able to do it pretty efficiently (in the sense
that the time should be negligible compared to computing
gradients each iteration).

I don't know where the hotspot in RStan is for this, but I'd
guess it's in reshaping everything to go into the fit
object. One approach we could take would be to do more work
lazily --- I've been thinking about that for the new interfaces.

- Bob

parts:
RStan saves the samples directly to an R vector.  So I don't think
there is much to be improved.  Also there is not reshaping for the final fit object, so there is no extra overload. 

But if rstan is unexpected slow for a model with not many parameters, we should take a look and see if there are places that can be proved.  So please let us know such specific cases. 

Jiqiang

On Thu, Jul 10, 2014 at 1:04 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
Nothing is being written out to .csv format and
read back in.  That would be super slow.
Everything communicates directly in memory through Rcpp.

Restricting the number of parameters output more efficiently
from the C++ Stan side is on our to-do list.  But R should
already be able to do it pretty efficiently (in the sense
that the time should be negligible compared to computing
gradients each iteration).

I don't know where the hotspot in RStan is for this, but I'd
guess it's in reshaping everything to go into the fit
object.  One approach we could take would be to do more work
lazily --- I've been thinking about that for the new interfaces.

- Bob

On Thursday, July 10, 2014 5:46:23 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:

full conditional density,

p(alpha | beta, x)

or just something proportional to it,

~ p(alpha | beta, x) ~ p(alpha, beta) | beta=const?

The former is what’s hard and the cause of my concern.

I think in all cases we can work with something proportional to p(alpha |beta, x).

The two steps are: a) simulate alpha from something proportional to p(alpha|beta,x),
let's say Stan can do this; and b) simulate beta from something proportional to 
p(beta|alpha,x), let's say something outside of Stan (say R, Python) can do this.
I don't think we ever need the full conditional, just something proportional.

I don't think the density proportional to p(alpha|beta,x) ever needs to be exposed from
Stan for this scheme to work. I just need to be able to read/write parameter/data efficiently.
It might be nice to get the density proportional to p(alpha|beta,x) but it is not necessary.

If it’s just
the latter that’s necessary then it’s no problem.  Apologies if I was
mistaken.

Thank you for chiming in, I've learned a lot from the Stan team's development
list and responses user questions and I appreciate the time you take to
resolve these questions.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request for rstan
parts:
The two steps are: a) simulate alpha from something proportional to p(alpha|beta,x), 
let's say Stan can do this; and b) simulate beta from something proportional to  
p(beta|alpha,x), let's say something outside of Stan (say R, Python) can do this.
I don't think we ever need the full conditional, just something proportional.

I don't think the density proportional to p(alpha|beta,x) ever needs to be exposed from
Stan for this scheme to work. I just need to be able to read/write parameter/data efficiently.
It might be nice to get the density proportional to p(alpha|beta,x) but it is not necessary.

Now I’m hesitant again.  In order to, say, sample a conditional from within Stan we’d have
to compute the joint (proportional to the conditional).  No external program will be able to
do the same without accessing the density, at the very least.

    b ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
)

and it produces Stan code like:

data{
    int<lower=1> N;
    real y[N];
    real x[N];
}
parameters{
    real a;
    real b;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model{
    vector[N] mu;
    sigma ~ exponential( 1 );
    b ~ normal( 0 , 1 );
    a ~ normal( 0 , 10 );
for ( i in 1:N ) {

mu[i] <- a + b * x[i];
    }
    y ~ normal( mu , sigma );
}

It wouldn't be hard to tag nodes in this interface. It support a few posterior prediction functions:

* link() to get values of linear model(s) at each sample
* sim() to get samples from outcome at each sample
* postcheck() just computes posterior predictions for each case in the sample and plots them
* WAIC() to calculate WAIC

Anyway, if I can get a better idea what the desired functionality is, it might be easier to add it to my package than to write another front end. Or you folks can just fork my work, although I imagine learning my parsing algorithm (it uses templates to map distributions from R to Stan) would be as much work as writing your own.

Cool. We totally have to check that out.

For functionality:

1. Basically, the whole BUGS/JAGS language. Ideally,
something that would translate models in both of those
languages!

2. Something that would take in the data for the model,
figure out which values are "missing" and create a model
where the missing data are considered parameters and then
glue everything back together. I'm not even sure how
BUGS does this in terms of returns, since the missing data
can be part of bigger structures (at least in some cases).

3. Something that could compute the Markov blanket for
discrete parameters so that we could do discrete sampling
with Gibbs. This is a wide-open research area in terms of
how this will interact with HMC and how adaptation would work.

4. Whatever Andrew wants for model comparison, data simulation
and posterior predictive checks. Looks like you're a long way
down that road already.


For compatibility:

1. We want everything we build for Stan to work in
CmdStan and PyStan as well as RStan. So we couldn't
have dependencies to R or anything else that's not
BSD-compatibly licensed (specifically, no GPL).

- Bob

P.S. We're also interested in something similar for the
R expression language --- I know you've worked on that before,
too. We're working on implementing uncertainty estimation for
MLE and also doing marginal maximum likelihood. There are still
some issues in how we take uncertainty back from the unconstrained
parameters to the constrained --- the best idea so far is to
use the normal approximation to generate samples around the mode
then transform back to the constrained space.
